passage: In Jamal's room in Nairobi, the guitar case wore a soft coat of dust. Jin, who had come over to borrow a charger, looked at it, then at the laptop still open at lesson four of an online coding course, then at the running shoes by the door. “Three things,” Jin said. “None finished.” Jamal shrugged. “The next one will be different.” He pulled up a video about making music on a laptop and his eyes lit up, exactly as they had for the guitar. Jin didn't say anything. Later, walking home, Jamal caught himself thinking that he always started well and never got to the end, and it felt oddly like a fact about himself.

qa.q: At which lesson was the coding course left?
qa.a: The coding course was left at lesson four.

qa.q: Why did Jamal's eyes light up at the music video?
qa.a: Jamal felt fresh excitement, the same as he felt for the guitar, because a new idea is more thrilling than pushing an old one through its dull stretch.

qa.q: What could Jamal try before starting the music idea?
qa.a: Choose one of the three older projects, do a small piece of it each day for two weeks, and only then decide about the new idea.

qa.q: How does Jin see the three unfinished projects?
qa.a: Jin notices the pattern kindly and says “None finished” without judging, but Jin may worry that Jamal is starting to see himself as someone who never finishes.

grounding: A teenager has several half-finished projects and a new idea feels more exciting, which builds a self-image as a non-finisher.

passage: The after-school club sign-up sheet went round again on Monday, and Ayesha wrote her name under Robotics. Indu, the coordinator, looked at the list. Ayesha had joined the chess club, the choir and the drama group since July, each for about three weeks. “I'm just a person who never finishes anything,” Ayesha said lightly, but her eyes stayed on the table. Indu didn't argue or give a speech. Indu asked, “Which one did you miss most after leaving?” Ayesha thought. “Chess. I liked the puzzle days.” Indu wrote “chess, term project: finish the ladder” in a small notebook and slid the notebook across. Ayesha looked at the page for a long moment, then crossed out Robotics.

qa.q: Which clubs had Ayesha joined since July?
qa.a: Ayesha had joined the chess club, the choir and the drama group.

qa.q: What does Ayesha's light tone and lowered eyes suggest she feels?
qa.a: Ayesha is hiding some hurt and shame under the light tone; the belief “never finishes anything” seems to weigh on Ayesha.

qa.q: What turning point in the scene makes Ayesha cross out Robotics?
qa.a: Indu asked which club Ayesha missed most, and Ayesha named chess, so a real interest replaced another new sign-up.

qa.q: What might Indu be thinking while writing in the notebook?
qa.a: Indu is probably gentle and hopeful, choosing a question over a lecture so Ayesha can arrive at the answer.

grounding: A teenager who has started and dropped many activities begins to see themselves as a non-finisher.
